newsitem.title: ITALY: Enel, Deutsche Telekom in talks - paper.
newsitem.headline: Enel, Deutsche Telekom in talks - paper.

text.p: Italian state electricity utility Enel and Deutsche Telekom are in talks over entering Italy's mobile phone market together, Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera said on Wednesday.
A spokesman for Enel declined to comment on the report saying: "At the moment we are talking with different people but we will only say something when we are ready."

Enel chairman Chicco Testa said separately to reporters in Rome: "It is no mystery that Enel is interested in entering the sector. I have already started having numerous contacts but I have no appointment planned with the German or French representative."
Top Enel managers have held talks with potential foreign partners including U.S. and Asian operators.
Corriere said Enel had singled out Deutsche Telekom as a potential technological partner.

It said the first step if they teamed up would be to compete for Italy's third mobile phone licence when that is tendered, which Posts and Telecoms Minister Antonio Maccanico has promised should be offered before the summer.
Corriere also said Deutsche Telekom chief executive Ron Sommer was due to be in Rome on Wednesday to meet Maccanico.
Industry sources confirmed Sommer was in Rome, as were representatives of France Telecom.
Italy is becoming a potential battleground for international telecoms companies.
British Telecom has already allied with broadcaster Mediaset for the third licence, and France Telecom recently teamed up with information technology group Olivetti on Infostrada.
Germany's Mannesmann and U.S. groups Air Touch and Bell Atlantic form part of the consortiums controlling second GSM operator Omnitel, which is mainly controlled by Olivetti.
Enel has extensive networks covering nine tenths of Italy which can be used both for fixed telephony and mobile phones.

Running this network represents hundreds of billions of lire in investment and management costs for Enel, and given the liberalisation of the telecoms sector, the state-controlled utility sees advantages in developing business in mobile and fixed line telephone services.
Enel has always maintained it would do this with technological and financial partners.

Despite the utility declining to comment, industry sources said the possibility of a link-up with Deutsche Telekom was credible, noting that 30 percent of Italy's international telephone traffic is with Germany.
